title: Iktomi and the Muskrat

setting.period: A Dakota story, told on the Great Plains for many generations

provenance.rights: The text is our own retelling of a Dakota Iktomi story, written for Omramo; it does not use the wording of the cited edition. The cited edition is in the US public domain (published before 1931); other territories not verified. Legal review pending (PRD Q23).

culturalReview.reason: Indigenous story (Dakota). Some Dakota and Lakota families tell Iktomi stories only in winter; a Dakota consultant must advise whether and how we publish it, and check every card.

geography.lesson: The northern Great Plains of North America are open grass country with prairie lakes and big rivers such as the Missouri. The Dakota live there today.

culture.lesson: Sharing food with a visitor is the Dakota way, as the Dakota writer Zitkala-Ša says herself. Iktomi the trickster teaches by doing things wrong: people laugh at him, and learn.

moral.lesson: Iktomi wants to keep everything and still look generous, and he ends with nothing. Sharing would have cost him half a pot; greed costs him all of it. He learns the right words, but will he remember them?
moral.reflectionQuestion: Iktomi knew the right thing to say all along. Why do you think he did not say it?

moral: Share what you have, for greed can lose you the whole pot.

cover.alt: Iktomi runs along the shore of a prairie lake with a big stone on his back, while a small muskrat swims straight across the water.

card.label: Character · the trickster
card.title: Iktomi
card.body: In Dakota stories Iktomi is a spider trickster who can look like a man. He does things the wrong way, and people laugh at him and learn.
card.portraitAlt: Iktomi in a fringed deerskin jacket, with red bands wrapped round his two long braids, hugging a cooking pot and looking sideways.

card.label: Character · the visitor from the lake
card.title: Muskrat
card.body: He comes out of the lake dripping wet and greets Iktomi as a friend. His legs are short, but nobody on the prairie swims better.
card.portraitAlt: Muskrat, small, round and dark brown, sitting up with wet whiskers among green cattails at the edge of the lake.

cultureNote.text: The Dakota live on the northern Great Plains, a country of tall grass, prairie lakes and big rivers such as the Missouri. Many Dakota families live there today, in South Dakota, North Dakota, Minnesota and Nebraska.

cultureNote.label: From the Dakota
cultureNote.text: Zitkala-Ša, the Dakota writer who set this story down, says that inviting a visitor to share your food was the custom of her people. Being generous is still greatly honoured among the Dakota today.

cultureNote.label: From the Great Plains
cultureNote.text: Muskrats live in lakes and marshes across North America. They heap up cattails and mud into a dome in the water, and the door is underneath, so they swim in and out unseen.

cultureNote.label: From the Dakota
cultureNote.text: Zitkala-Ša, a Yankton Dakota woman, wrote these stories down in 1901 so that all children could read them. The Dakota tell Iktomi stories today, and some families tell them only on winter nights.

paras: ^Iktomi sat by a prairie lake with a whole pot of fish.
All around him the grass of the <tap:great-plains>Great Plains</tap> ran out to the edge of the sky. Wild rice stood thick in the shallows, and an old willow leaned over the water.
<name:iktomi>Iktomi</name> was a trickster, who liked playing tricks far better than working. Meals did not come to him every day, but today he had more boiled fish than he could eat in two.
He stirred it with his horn spoon. He sniffed the steam. He hummed a dance song, and he did not look up once.
<say:muskrat*>“Good day, my friend!”</say> said a voice from the wild rice.
Iktomi jumped so hard that he nearly swallowed his spoon. There at his elbow stood <name:muskrat>Muskrat</name>, sleek and dripping, fresh from the lake.
<say:iktomi*>“Good day,”</say> said Iktomi, and that was all he said.

Now, among the Dakota, when a visitor finds you eating, you ask him to sit down and <tap:guest-custom>share the meal</tap>. “Come and sit, my friend. There is plenty for two.” Iktomi knew it as well as he knew his own name.
Muskrat smiled and waited to be asked. Iktomi hummed louder and tapped time on the rim of the pot.
Muskrat looked at his wet toes. The lake behind him seemed a very good place to be.
Iktomi wanted every last fish for himself. He also wanted to look like the most generous fellow on the prairie.

He put down his spoon. <say:iktomi*>“My friend, I have a fine idea!”</say> he cried. <say:iktomi>“We shall run a race, from the far side of the lake back to this fire, and the winner eats the fish.”</say>
<say:muskrat*>“Race you?”</say> said Muskrat. <say:muskrat>“You have long legs, and look at mine. They are no longer than your thumb.”</say>
<say:iktomi*>“Then I will run with a heavy rock tied on my back,”</say> said Iktomi grandly. <say:iktomi>“Nobody can call that unfair.”</say>
They walked round to the far side of the lake, where grey stones lay in the shallows. Iktomi chose the biggest, to show how fair he was.
He spread out his blanket and rolled the stone into it. Muskrat pushed from below, Iktomi heaved from above, and up it went onto his back.
<say:iktomi*>“Light as a duck feather,”</say> said Iktomi, with his knees shaking.
Far across the water, a thin thread of smoke showed where the pot was waiting. The first to reach the fire would win.
<say:muskrat*>“Ready?”</say> asked Muskrat politely. <say:iktomi*>“<pop:1.3>Go!</pop>”</say> shouted Iktomi, and he was off.
^The shore of the lake was much longer than it looked.

<name:iktomi>Iktomi</name> ran through mud that sucked at his moccasins. He ran through reeds that slapped his face. The stone went thump, thump, thump against his back, and the mosquitoes sang in both his ears.
Halfway round he stopped to puff, and he looked across the water. Nothing moved on the other shore. No grass shook. No small brown runner hurried along it.
<say:iktomi*>“Poor fellow,”</say> said Iktomi. <say:iktomi>“He is so slow that I cannot even see him. I shall eat one fish for him.”</say>
He laughed, hitched up his stone and ran on.
But <name:muskrat>Muskrat</name> was not on the other shore. Muskrat was not on any shore at all.
Nobody had said which way to go, so he had slipped into the lake without a splash. Now he swam straight across the middle, with only his nose and whiskers showing.
Out among the cattails stood his house, a round <tap:reed-lodge>lodge of reeds</tap> heaped up in the water. He had dived and paddled here since he was a kit no bigger than a duck’s egg.
A long V of ripples spread out behind him, and the thread of smoke grew nearer with every stroke.
The afternoon was nearly gone when Iktomi staggered up to the willow tree.
There lay the ashes, still warm. There lay his horn spoon. But there was no pot, no fish and no Muskrat.
Iktomi let go of the blanket. Down came the stone, <pop:1.3>thump</pop>, right on his toe.
He hopped round the ashes on one foot, howling. Then he sat down and held his toe in both hands.
<say:iktomi*>“He swam!”</say> he groaned. <say:iktomi>“Of course he swam. And I carried a rock round a lake! A pot shared is half a pot. A pot raced for is no pot at all.”</say>
All that running had made him thirsty. He limped to the lake and bent down to drink.
Then he stared. Down in the deep green water sat Muskrat, with the pot between his paws, picking a fish clean.
<say:iktomi*>“So that is where you are hiding!”</say> cried <name:iktomi>Iktomi</name>. He plunged in his arm up to the shoulder and caught a handful of cold water.
Somebody laughed. The laugh came from over his head.
Iktomi looked up. On a branch of the old willow sat the real Muskrat with the real pot. The one in the lake was only his picture in the water.
<say:iktomi*>“Muskrat! Dear, kind Muskrat!”</say> called Iktomi. <say:iktomi>“Throw me down a little. One fish. Even one bone would do!”</say>
He tipped back his head and opened his mouth as wide as it would go.
Muskrat chose a bone and dropped it with care. It hit Iktomi on the nose, plink, and fell in the grass. Iktomi was on his knees at once, hunting for it.

Muskrat laughed until the branch shook. <say:muskrat*>“Next time a friend comes while you are eating,”</say> he said, <say:muskrat>“try saying this: ‘Come and sit, my friend. There is plenty for two.’ It is not hard.”</say>
Iktomi limped home across the prairie with an empty stomach and a toe as fat as a plum. Behind him, in the willow, Muskrat was scraping the pot.

All the way he practised. <say:iktomi*>“Come and sit, my friend. There is plenty for two,”</say> he told a meadowlark on a grass stem. <say:iktomi>“Come and sit, my friend,”</say> he told a grasshopper, and a grey stone, and the first pale star.
By the time he reached home he had it perfectly. He lay down very pleased with himself.
And by morning, the <tap:storyteller>storytellers</tap> say, he had forgotten every word.

sourceNotes: This is our own retelling, written for Omramo, of a Dakota Iktomi story. It is not the wording of any
earlier edition, and it is not a traditional telling by a Dakota storyteller.
Documented source: Zitkala-Sa (Gertrude Simmons Bonnin, Yankton Dakota), "Old Indian Legends" (1901),
chapter "Iktomi and the Muskrat". Project Gutenberg ebook #338, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/338
(US public domain; the author died in 1938; other territories not verified).
The 1901 title word 'Indian' appears only in this citation, never in the story or the cards.
Source read: yes, through the Gutenberg mirror (gutenberg.pglaf.org/3/3/338/338.txt), as a summary;
the retelling was then written fresh. A source-check pass should still compare for echoes of her wording.
SOFTENED: in the source the muskrat drops a sharp bone into Iktomi's open throat and he almost chokes
to death. Here the bone bounces off his nose. In the source Iktomi also nearly chokes with fright at
the first greeting; here he nearly swallows his spoon.
LEFT OUT: the source's greeting word (a stereotype in English today); Iktomi saying he took the voice
for a spirit; the muskrat mocking him for carrying the weight; the description of Iktomi's face paint.
DEPARTS FROM THE SOURCE: (1) Race terms. Source: if Iktomi wins he need not share, if the muskrat wins
he gets half. Ours: the winner eats the fish. (2) Source: Iktomi drops the stone part-way and sprints.
Ours: he carries it all the way and drops it on his toe (invented comic beat). (3) Source: he peers
into the water and begs the reflection for a bone. Ours: he bends to drink and plunges an arm in.
(4) Source: he laments not sharing 'like a real Dakota'. Ours: 'as anybody should', because we did not
want to put a claim about who is a real Dakota into a trickster's mouth without advice. (5) The last
page (practising the sentence on the way home, forgetting it by morning) is our invention, not hers.
(6) 'Nobody had said which way to go' is our line; the source simply has the muskrat swim.
(7) Muskrat's line about his short legs and the muskrat lodge passage are ours (natural history).
KEPT FROM THE SOURCE: the lake, the wild rice, the large willow, the pot of boiled fish, the horn
spoon, the humming and drumming on the pot, the stone fetched from the far side of the lake and wrapped
in his blanket, the reflection, the tree, the bone, and the muskrat's closing advice (in our words).
CHANGED FROM THE EDITORIAL PLAN: the plan had a cottonwood; the source has a willow, so ours is a willow.
The plan started and ended the race at the fire, which leaves the muskrat nothing to swim across; as in
the source, the race now starts on the far side of the lake and ends at the pot.
FOR THE DAKOTA CONSULTANT - first question: may this story be published in an app that is read in
every season? Some Dakota and Lakota families tell Iktomi stories only in winter. CONTENT_PLAN 1.3
excludes narratives told only in a certain season; if that applies here, the story must be withdrawn
or handled as the consultant advises (for example a note on when such stories are told).
Check 2: the name and spelling 'Iktomi' (also written Unktomi / Inktomi in Dakota dialects), and the
spelling and use of 'Zitkala-Sa' with her English name.
Check 3: 'Dakota (Yankton)'. The Yankton (Ihanktonwan) are also called Western Dakota or Nakota;
which name should the app show? Is the map pin (43.0 N, 98.5 W, near Yankton land) acceptable?
Check 4: the narrator's sentence 'among the Dakota, when a visitor finds you eating, there is one right
thing to say'. The source calls it 'the custom of the plains people'. Is our wording true and welcome?
Check 5: the hospitality sentence itself, 'Sit beside me, my friend, and share my food' (our wording).
Check 6: card 'storyteller': the sentence 'some families tell them only on winter nights', and whether
to say it at all; that she wrote the stories down in 1901 so that all children could read them.
Check 7: card 'guest-custom': 'Being generous is still greatly honoured among the Dakota today.'
Check 8: card 'great-plains': the states named (South Dakota, North Dakota, Minnesota, Nebraska);
Dakota communities also live in Montana and in Canada. Should the card name them?
Check 9: Iktomi's character card: 'a spider trickster who can look like a man' (the source says
'spider fairy'), and 'people laugh at him and learn'. Is 'trickster' the right English word?
Check 10: Iktomi is drawn as a man in deerskin, as the source describes. Is any drawing of him welcome?
The art brief leaves off the face paint the source describes and keeps beadwork to plain bands,
so that no real design is copied. Advise on paint, beadwork, hair and the red hair bands.
Check 11: 'He hummed a dance song': a detail from the source. Acceptable for a comic character?
Check 12: words used in English: moccasins, lodge (for the muskrat's house only), prairie, kit.
No Dakota-language word is used except the name Iktomi. No tipi is named in the text; the art brief
allows one plain tipi far off. Advise.
Check 13: wild rice at a prairie lake (from the source); the horn spoon (buffalo horn in the source).
Facts for an editor: muskrat lodges of cattails and mud with underwater entrances; a young muskrat
is a kit; western meadowlarks and willows on the northern plains.
SOURCE CHECK (18 Nov 2026, against Gutenberg #338 on the mirror): the first draft stayed close to her
wording in the race offer, the stone, the begging for a bone, the lament and the hospitality sentence.
All were reworded: the hospitality line is now ours ('Come and sit, my friend. There is plenty for two.'),
a paraphrase of the custom she states, not a quotation and not a Dakota formula. Consultant: check 4 and 5
above now refer to this wording. The lament is ours ('A pot shared is half a pot').
CORRECTION to departure (6): in the source the two agree to run on opposite sides of the lake, so the
muskrat's swim breaks the agreed course. Ours says nobody had said which way to go, so that he is not
cheating. Further departures: the source's fire is already out (ours smokes, and the smoke is the goal);
her muskrat says Iktomi is nimble as a deer; her stone is half-buried in the shallows; her lake is white;
the spoon left by the ashes, the mud and the mosquitoes are ours.
Status: DRAFT. Text review pending. Cultural review (required: Dakota consultant) pending.

palette.mood: A wide pale prairie sky over lake blue and gold-green grass, with warm earth reds in small notes (the hair bands, the blanket stripe, the fire). Quiet, airy and a little comic; the sky is most of every picture.

artBrief.light: Clear summer daylight from the upper left in every picture; big white cumulus clouds. The last scene (scene-tree) is late afternoon with a pale gold sky. Never night, never a dark sky: this is a light story and dark text sits on the sky.
world: The northern Great Plains (the Yankton Dakota country near the Missouri River, today's South Dakota): gently rolling open grassland to a far, level horizon. Tall-grass and mixed prairie, gold-green in summer, with a few prairie flowers. No mountains, no forest, no desert.

A prairie lake: shallow, still, pale blue, with soft muddy edges. In the shallows stand wild rice (tall thin grass with feathery seed heads), cattails (brown sausage-shaped heads) and bulrushes. Grey rounded stones lie in the shallows on the far side.

The tree is one large old willow leaning out over the water, as in the source: a thick grey trunk, long narrow leaves, low strong branches. Trees grow only at the water; the grassland itself is open. A few low willows may stand along the shore.

The muskrat is a real animal: small (about the size of a rabbit), round-backed, dark glossy brown with a paler belly, tiny ears almost hidden in fur, small dark eyes, long whiskers, small clever front paws, and a long THIN scaly tail flattened side to side. Not a beaver: no paddle tail, no big orange teeth.
A muskrat lodge: a rounded dome about a metre high of heaped cattails, reeds and mud, standing in shallow water among cattails. No door shows; the entrance is under the water.

The pot is a plain dark round-bodied cooking pot with a wire handle, sitting on the ground beside a small fire of sticks (later only grey ashes). The fish are whole small boiled fish. The spoon is a dark horn spoon with a curved handle. Draw nothing ceremonial near the food.

The blanket is a plain wool blanket in one earth colour with one or two simple stripes at the ends. It becomes the sling for the stone: the stone is tied in the blanket and carried on his back, the knot on his chest.

Far off on the grass, at most one plain tipi (a tall cone of pale hide with poles crossing at the top, no painted designs). Accurate for the Yankton Dakota; keep it tiny and plain, or leave it out. This is flagged for the consultant.

Small prairie life for the edges: a western meadowlark (yellow breast with a black V) on a grass stem, a grasshopper, dragonflies, a few ducks far out on the lake, mosquitoes as tiny specks around Iktomi in the race scene.

Dress follows the Dakota writer's own description of Iktomi (deerskin, fringes, beaded moccasins, hair bands). Keep beadwork to plain bands of two or three colours; do not copy or invent detailed designs. Leave his face unpainted until the Dakota consultant advises.

Avoid: feather war bonnets or any feathers in the hair, totem poles, tomahawks, bows as decoration, pipes, eagle feathers, medicine wheels, dreamcatchers or any sacred object; birchbark canoes; desert mesas and cactus; buffalo stampedes; horses; painted tipis; a face in profile with a hawk-nose caricature; red skin tones (draw warm natural brown skin); a stoic or fierce expression. No spider body, legs or web on Iktomi anywhere. No log cabins, no metal tools beyond the pot.

characters.iktomi: A slim, loose-limbed man about three heads tall with a lively, vain, comic face: raised eyebrows, small plain eyes, a mouth that is pleased with itself until Part II. Warm brown skin. Long black hair parted in the middle, in two braids that hang forward over his shoulders, each wrapped with red bands. A brown deerskin jacket with a plain band of beads, brown deerskin leggings with long soft fringes, small beaded moccasins. No face paint (pending advice). Signature details: the horn spoon in his hand in Part I; the stone in the blanket on his back in the race; one sore toe held up at the end.
characters.muskrat: A small, round, dark brown muskrat, sleek and wet, with long whiskers, tiny ears and a long thin tail. He stands or sits upright like a polite visitor, front paws together. Friendly small dark eyes; a patient smile in Part I, an open laugh in the tree. No clothes. Signature detail: drops of water on his fur and whiskers.

scene-lake.unfolded: Far: a level horizon of gold-green grass under a wide pale blue sky with two or three white clouds. Middle: the pale blue lake across both panes, wild rice and cattails at its edge, the old willow at the far right edge leaning over the water. Near, on the trailing (right) half: Iktomi sitting on the ground by a small fire with the pot between his feet and the horn spoon in his hand, looking only into the pot; the muskrat's wet head and shoulders rising from the wild rice at the water's edge beside him. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are calm pale sky above a low line of grass and water.
scene-lake.folded: Iktomi's face in the middle, bent over the pot with the spoon, humming; the muskrat standing dripping at his elbow, looking up; wild rice behind and pale sky at the top for the words.

scene-race.unfolded: Far: a huge pale sky with tall white cumulus clouds over a very low horizon. Middle: the lake on the left and its shore curving away in a long arc of mud, reeds and grass, with a thin thread of smoke rising far across the water. Near, on the trailing (right) half: Iktomi running bent double with the big grey stone tied in the blanket on his back, braids flying, mud to his ankles, a few specks of mosquitoes about his head. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are open pale sky.
scene-race.folded: Iktomi's puffing face in the middle, cheeks blown out, the blanket-wrapped stone rising behind his shoulders, reeds at each side and pale sky above.

scene-swim.unfolded: A low viewpoint just above the water. Far: a thin line of far bank with the willow tiny on it and a thread of smoke rising beside it, under a pale sky. Middle: wide calm pale blue water with soft reflections of clouds; at the right edge a round reed lodge among cattails. Near, on the trailing (right) half: the muskrat swimming straight towards the far bank, only nose, eyes, whiskers and the line of his back showing, a long clean V of ripples opening behind him. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are pale sky and palest water, calm for the words.
scene-swim.folded: The muskrat's head in the middle, seen from the front and a little above, swimming towards us with whiskers spread and a V of ripples behind; pale water and sky above.

scene-tree.unfolded: Late afternoon with a PALE gold sky, never dark. Far: the level grass horizon and soft gold clouds. Middle: still water holding clear reflections. Near, on the trailing (right) half: the old willow leaning out over the lake; high on a strong branch the muskrat sitting with the pot held between his paws, laughing; below, Iktomi kneeling at the water's edge and staring down at the muskrat's reflection in the water, the dropped stone and blanket and the grey ashes beside him. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are open pale gold sky above quiet water.
scene-tree.folded: Iktomi in the lower middle with his head tipped back and his mouth open; the muskrat above him on the willow branch with the pot, holding one small fish bone over him; pale gold sky behind the leaves.

pictures.great-plains: One wide view of open gold-green prairie with a single blue lake in the middle and a huge sky of white clouds above; no people, no buildings.
pictures.guest-custom: One plain dark cooking pot of fish on the grass with two horn spoons leaning side by side against it, as if set out for two.
pictures.reed-lodge: One round dome of heaped brown reeds and cattails standing in still blue-green water, with a muskrat swimming towards it and a small V of ripples.
pictures.storyteller: One open book lying on a plain striped wool blanket, with the warm glow of a small fire behind it. No portrait of a real person, no objects beyond these.

portraits.iktomi: Half figure, hugging the pot to his chest with both arms and looking sideways out of the corner of his eye, horn spoon sticking up from his fist; fringed deerskin jacket, two braids with red bands; warm gold and earth-red light behind.
portraits.muskrat: The muskrat sitting upright among green cattails at the water's edge, front paws together, whiskers wet, with a friendly patient look; pale lake blue behind.

artBrief.cover: The race in one picture: in the foreground Iktomi running along the shore, bent under the big stone in his blanket and looking very pleased with himself; behind him, out on the pale lake, the small dark head of the muskrat swimming straight across with a long V of ripples; a huge pale sky with white clouds above.
